segments.text: Before race: where the fear came from
People often ask why the targeting of Black, Brown and Native people has lasted so long, and whether some forgotten origin explains it.
The record gives a clearer answer: modern race is recent, it was written into law on purpose, and it has been defended by whatever argument was handy, including scripture and science.
The ancient world sorted people differently
Slavery is ancient, but for most of history it was not based on skin color.
Greeks, Romans, Egyptians, Africans, Arabs and Europeans enslaved people taken in war, sold for debt, or born to enslaved mothers, and enslaved people came from every region.
The English word slave itself comes from Slav, because so many Eastern Europeans were enslaved in the Middle Ages.
Historian Frank Snowden showed that Greek and Roman writers described Africans with curiosity and sometimes admiration, without the idea of a fixed racial ranking.
Race was written into law (1452–1705)
The idea that some people are naturally meant to be owned was spelled out step by step:
1452–1455: Pope Nicholas V's bulls Dum Diversas and Romanus Pontifex authorized Portugal's king to conquer “Saracens and pagans” and reduce them to perpetual slavery.
Portugal's African slave trade grew under them.
1493: Inter caetera gave Spain lands “discovered” in the Americas.
These bulls became the Doctrine of Discovery, which the U.S. Supreme Court adopted in Johnson v. M'Intosh (1823) to deny Native nations full ownership of their land.
The Vatican repudiated the doctrine in 2023.
The Supreme Court has not.
1662: Virginia ruled that a child follows the condition of the mother, so children of enslaved women, including children of their enslavers, were born enslaved.

1667–1705: Virginia declared that baptism does not free a slave (1667), that killing an enslaved person during “correction” was not a felony (1669), banned interracial marriage (1691), and gathered everything into the 1705 slave codes.
France's Code Noir (1685) did the same for its colonies.
Dividing people who might unite
In 1676, Bacon's Rebellion brought white indentured servants and enslaved Africans together in an armed revolt against Virginia's government.

In the decades that followed, Virginia's laws gave poor white people small privileges (freedom dues, the right to bear arms, the right to strike a Black person) while taking rights away from all Black people, free or enslaved.
That the laws changed is documented.
Historian Edmund Morgan argued that the elite used race on purpose to keep poor white and Black people from uniting again.
Others think the shift had more to do with the falling cost of enslaved Africans compared with English servants.
Most agree the effect was the same.
The practice came first, the ideas followed
In 1944 the Trinidadian historian Eric Williams wrote that “slavery was not born of racism: rather, racism was the consequence of slavery.”
Ibram X. Kendi's Stamped from the Beginning (2016) traces the same pattern over five centuries: racist ideas were developed to defend policies that were already profitable.
Thomas Jefferson, who enslaved more than 600 people over his life, offered Black inferiority “as a suspicion only” in his Notes on the State of Virginia (1785).
Within decades, “scientists” were measuring skulls to prove it (see the module on science).
What the fear was really about
The fear was real.
It was fear of revolt, of revenge, and of losing power at the ballot box:
Haiti, 1791–1804: enslaved people overthrew French rule and founded the first free Black republic.
France later forced Haiti to pay 150 million francs (reduced to 90 million) for its own freedom, a debt Haiti paid off over about 120 years.
Nat Turner's rebellion, 1831: afterward, Virginia and other states tightened bans on teaching Black people to read and on Black preachers and gatherings.
Reconstruction, 1867–1877: Black men voted and held office, and South Carolina's lower house had a Black majority.
White-supremacist violence ended it, including the 1898 coup in Wilmington, North Carolina, where an elected biracial government was overthrown by force.
“Replacement”: Madison Grant's The Passing of the Great Race (1916) warned that white Americans were being outbred.
It helped pass the 1924 immigration quotas.
The same fear, renamed the “Great Replacement,” was cited by the killers in El Paso (2019) and Buffalo (2022).
How scripture was used, and misused
The “Curse of Ham.”
In Genesis 9:20–27, Noah curses Canaan, Ham's son, to be a servant.
The text says nothing about skin color or Africa.
Linking the curse to dark skin came much later and was spread by interpreters across several traditions.
By the 1800s it was a standard pro-slavery argument in American pulpits.
The “Slave Bible.”
In 1807 a British missionary society printed Select Parts of the Holy Bible, for the Use of the Negro Slaves.
It cut most of the Old Testament, including the Exodus story of freedom from slavery, and kept passages like “Servants, be obedient to them that are your masters.”
Scripture was also the strongest weapon against slavery: enslaved people sang of Moses and Exodus, and abolitionists from Frederick Douglass to the Black church built their case on it.
The Book of Enoch and modern race myths
1 Enoch is an ancient Jewish book that is part of the Bible of the Ethiopian Orthodox Church; fragments were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls, and the Letter of Jude (verses 14–15) quotes it.
It tells how angels called the Watchers came to earth, taught forbidden knowledge, and fathered giants (the Nephilim of Genesis 6).
It contains no teaching about race.
Modern movements have still built race stories on Genesis and Enoch.
We describe them so you can recognize them, not because they are true:
Christian Identity “two-seedline” theology, a white-supremacist doctrine claiming Jews and people of color descend from the serpent or from “pre-Adamic” races.
The Nation of Islam's story of Yakub, which teaches that a scientist named Yakub created white people thousands of years ago.
Some Hebrew Israelite groups teach that Black, Hispanic and Native Americans are the true Israelites and that others are cursed.
These stories mirror each other: each claims race is ancient, fixed and cosmic.
The historical record shows the opposite: race is recent, made by people, and can be unmade.
